messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Amina, a 21-year-old African American woman, came to treatment after several months of feeling increasingly unable to settle back into ordinary life following her deployment-related trauma. Before the event, she had been living in a disciplined, busy rhythm that fit her sense of herself: she worked as a counselor, kept close contact with people she had known before her service, and imagined that she would always be someone who could handle difficult situations. During the combat incident, that confidence was shattered in a way she still struggled to put into words. Helicopters overhead, once just part of the landscape of military life, became permanently tied to the moment when everything turned dangerous. She remembered the sound of aircraft arriving and circling, then the darkness that closed in around her when she could no longer orient herself the way she had before. In the aftermath, comments about family took on an unexpectedly sharp edge. When anyone mentioned home, parents, siblings, or the ordinary safety of family life, she was pulled back to the contrast between that world and the one in which she had been trapped. She could not hear those remarks as casual conversation anymore; they landed like reminders of what had been lost and what she had survived.

Over the following weeks, Amina began arranging her life around what felt manageable. She found herself avoiding dark spaces, particularly places where she could not immediately see who or what was around her. Even in her apartment, she kept lights on longer than she wanted to admit, and she hesitated before stepping into dim hallways or parking lots after dusk. Helicopter or aircraft sounds were especially difficult. If one passed overhead, her body would tense before she had time to think, and her attention narrowed to the sky and to the sense that something bad could happen again. She also found herself pulling away from people. Seeing individuals she had socialized with before the event, including former friends and acquaintances who expected her to resume the same easy familiarity, made her increasingly uncomfortable. She did not want to explain why she had become quieter and more guarded, so she started declining invitations and letting messages sit unanswered. Starting new friendships or relationships felt even harder. Amina worried that if she let someone close, they would eventually see how different she had become and would be disappointed by her distance. She told herself it was easier not to begin than to risk being known in that state.

Her avoidance began to affect both her work and her personal life in concrete ways. As a counselor, Amina had once felt steady in the role of listening, encouraging, and helping others sort through painful experiences. Now she questioned whether she could still do the work in the same way. She found herself comparing who she was before the trauma with who she was now and concluding, with a painful sense of finality, that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her. Even at work, she felt less like the competent young woman others had relied on and more like someone trying not to be noticed. She became wary of situations that might expose her to unexpected sounds or emotionally charged conversations, and she worried that colleagues would sense she was not the same. In private, she was equally hard on herself. Amina had come to believe there was something about her that had made the event happen, as if her own presence, judgment, or weakness had somehow marked her out. At other times she was seized by the more humiliating thought that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation at all. Those beliefs left her carrying not only fear, but a heavy sense of personal failure.

By the time she sought help, Amina was exhausted by how much of her life had narrowed. She had stopped reaching out to people she had once felt comfortable with, had avoided opening herself to new relationships, and had become increasingly selective about the media she consumed, steering clear of television programmes, films, and stories about similar events because even brief exposure could leave her unsettled and on guard. She knew these choices were shrinking her world, but she also felt they were the only way to keep the memories at a distance. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was no longer managing to keep the fear contained; it was following her into work, into conversations, and into the ordinary evening moments when a dark room or the distant sound of aircraft could suddenly make her feel as if she were back there again. More than anything, Amina was frightened that she would never feel like herself again. At the same time, she was hoping that treatment might help her regain a sense of safety and recover some version of the capable counselor and friend she had once been.
